big: Rohan spends ₹40,000 on his card and pays only the minimum due, ₹2,000. The bank is happy. He feels fine. Next month the interest begins to pile on the other ₹38,000.

lines: A card gives me weeks to pay. Where is the catch?
There is none, if you pay the whole statement by the due date. The trap is the minimum due, and borrowing for things that do not last.

title: Cards and loans
stops: Paying the full bill on time costs no interest
The minimum due clears the bill
A secured loan usually carries a lower rate
Borrowing is fine for any kind of spending
caps: On time and in full, a card is a short loan with no interest.
The minimum only keeps the account from being overdue. Interest runs on the rest.
The lender can take the asset behind a secured loan, so it charges less.
Borrow for things that last or grow, such as a home or education.

note: Card rates are among the highest in lending, so carrying a balance is costly.

q: Meena pays her full card statement by the due date every month. What does she pay in interest?
opts: A small fixed amount each month
Interest on the whole yearly spend
Interest only on the minimum due
why: There is no fixed monthly charge when the statement is cleared on time.
Paid in full by the due date, no interest is charged on purchases.
Interest does not build on a year of spending if she pays each bill in full.
The minimum due is not what interest is charged on.

q: Rohan pays only the minimum due on his card. What is the main result?
opts: Interest runs on the unpaid balance
The whole bill is cleared by the bank
His credit limit is doubled by the bank
His score rises at once, as a reward
why: The minimum avoids a late mark, but the rest keeps building interest.
The minimum is a small share of the bill, so the bill is not cleared.
Paying the minimum does not increase his limit.
Carrying a balance can strain his score, not lift it.

q: Why does a home loan usually cost less than a personal loan?
opts: Homes never lose any value over time
Personal loans are meant to be charged more as a rule
The home backs the loan, so risk is lower
Banks give home loans as a favour
why: Homes can lose value, so the lower rate comes from security instead.
Rates follow the lender's risk, and are not set as a form of punishment.
A secured loan is backed by an asset, so risk and rate are lower.
Banks lend to earn a return, so security is the real reason.

q: Meena already pays ₹30,000 in EMIs on a take-home of ₹90,000. A friend suggests a loan for a holiday. What is wise?
opts: Borrow, since holidays are good for mind and body
Take two loans so each EMI stays small
Skip her current EMIs to pay for the holiday
Hold off, since she is near a safe limit already
why: A holiday may be a joy, but borrowing for it adds cost with no lasting value.
Two loans add up to the same strain, and cost more in fees.
Skipping EMIs brings penalties and damages her credit record.
Thirty thousand is a third of her pay, so more debt for a trip is not wise.

pts: Pay the full statement by the due date and a card costs no interest.
The minimum due is a trap. Interest runs on everything left.
Borrow for things that last or grow. Keep total EMIs within a safe share.
